text:
The Las Vegas Raiders head into their Week 1 game against the Miami Dolphins on Sept. 13 with a question mark surrounding Ashton Jeanty. Before the preseason finale against the San Francisco 49ers, Jeanty suffered an ankle injury.

Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak is expecting Jeanty to play, but he did leave room for the second-year running back to miss the game if his ankle isn't 100 percent ready to go.

Advertisement

"Still on the mend, still working to get him back," Kubiak told reporters on Aug. 28. "We got another week to assess how he's going to look going into this first game, but we're counting on him."

For now, if Jeanty does miss the game, the Raiders would be counting on Mike Washington Jr. to carry the load. However, one veteran running back issued a message to the Silver and Black that he'd be willing to help.

While speaking to 8 News Now's Madyson Marie, former Los Angeles Chargers running back Austin Ekeler expressed interest in playing for the Raiders.

"I'm unemployed right now," Ekeler said in an Aug. 28 video. "Being in my hometown anyway would be a dream for my family. I know that. Is the situation right? We'll have to see. How is Jeanty feeling? Do they need another guy?"

Advertisement

After leaving Los Angeles, Ekeler spent the last two seasons with the Washington Commanders, and the production wasn't the best. Ekeler had 91 carries for 410 yards and scored four touchdowns in 14 games for the Commanders, per StatMuse.

What Austin Ekeler Could Bring to the Raiders

Nonetheless, the 31-year-old noted the role he would be open to filling with the Raiders, should Las Vegas be interested in bringing him back to the AFC West.

"If I'm on a team, I'm going to be your third-down back," Ekeler added. "I'm going to be your two-minute guy. I'm going to be protecting your quarterback in passing situations. That's where I'm best.

Advertisement

"I'm best in passing situations. I can still run the ball. I can return kicks, absolutely. But my biggest strength is that. So if that presents itself, sure. If not, it's all good."

Klint Kubiak on Las Vegas' Running Back Situation

The Raiders look to have an impressive running game heading into the season with Jeanty and Washington. Kubiak spoke about the duo that can take pressure off the quarterback and boost the passing game. Furthermore, it doesn't sound like he's looking to sign a veteran free agent.

"I think that they're both going to prepare to play a lot of football," Kubiak told reporters. "As these games unfold, you react to the game. I think we got two guys that we're really excited about. We got some younger guys that we're really excited about too."

Advertisement

If the Raiders do decide to give Jeanty a rest for Week 1 and lean on Washington, the rookie running back might be ready for that task.

Last season, while playing for the Arkansas Razorbacks, Washington played 571 total snaps, earning a 78.3 overall PFF grade. Moreover, the 23-year-old carried the ball 167 times for 1,066 rushing yards and eight touchdowns.

He also averaged 6.4 yards per attempt and forced 34 missed tackles as a runner. Meanwhile, in the passing game, Washington caught 28 passes on 36 targets for 226 receiving yards and one touchdown.

text:
BEREA, Ohio -- The Cleveland Browns on Sunday trimmed their roster from four quarterbacks to three ahead of the NFL's cut-down deadline at 6 p.m. ET Sunday but did so without cutting or trading a passer.

Instead, Cleveland placed Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve and designated him to return with a back injury. The Browns will carry Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders and rookie Taylen Green as the quarterbacks on their initial 53-man roster.

Gabriel injured his back in Cleveland's preseason-closing win against the New England Patriots on Thursday night, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter. Gabriel had pain Saturday and underwent an MRI. He will be eligible to return after the first four games of the regular season.

The No. 94 pick in the 2025 draft, Gabriel started and played the first half of the preseason finale, throwing three touchdown passes. First-year coach Todd Monken was complimentary of Gabriel, who also started six games as a rookie.

authors: Adam Pfeifer, Dwain McFarland, Kendall Valenzuela, Sam Wallace
description:
All offseason, the fantasy football community has been debating whether Jayden Reed or Matthew Golden will emerge as the Green Bay Packers' WR2.
It’s Christian Watson season, y’all.

Christian Watson: WR1 If you are looking for the next breakout fantasy wideout, Watson checks seemingly every box.
text:
All offseason, the fantasy football community has been debating whether Jayden Reed or Matthew Golden will emerge as the Green Bay Packers' WR2. Both are intriguing, late-round upside swings, though there remains some uncertainty about their week-to-week role. There is no doubt, however, who the alpha in this offense will be.

It’s Christian Watson season, y’all.

For much of his career, Watson has flashed so much upside. Tons of touchdowns and fantasy points in certain stretches have unfortunately been paired with missed time due to injury. That was once again the case this past season when Watson returned halfway through the year following a late 2024 ACL tear. But Watson is now fully healthy, and following a four-year, $110.5 million contract extension, he is set to play the largest role of his career, not just for the Green Bay offense—but for fantasy teams as well.

A Sign Of What’s To Come

A 2024 late-season ACL tear sidelined Watson for the first seven games of last season, presenting serious risk as a fantasy option. But when he made his debut in Week 8, Watson wasted no time showing his immense upside. From Weeks 8-18, Watson ran 72% of the routes, while posting a 23% TPRR and 20% target share. During that stretch, Watson was the WR22 in fantasy points per game (13.2), but the underlying metrics prove that, with added volume, he can do so much more.

Watson Weeks 8-18:

17.5 Yd/Rec (2nd)

2.54 YPRR (8th)

11 plays of 20-plus yards (10th)

6 TDs (5th)

Despite ranking just 33rd in targets during that stretch (55), Watson ranked 14th in receiving yards (608), showcasing his huge play potential. Watson was fantasy’s WR21 on a PPG basis upon his return, while his 0.57 fantasy points per route were good for fifth-best among all wideouts. But keep in mind that Watson wasn’t always a full-time player during that stretch. He dealt with shoulder issues down the stretch, limiting him to just 56.3% of the routes from Weeks 15-17. If you look at the games where he ran at least 70% of the routes, Watson averaged closer to 15 PPR PPG.

Watson was once again mostly used down the field, ranking sixth in the league in aDOT from Week 8 on (18.0), while running go routes just under 22% of the time. Watson’s skill set is always going to lend itself to explosive plays deep down the field. But he can also do more than that.

And for the first time in his career, he’ll be asked to prove it.

Email Address

By registering or logging in, you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Christian Watson: WR1

If you are looking for the next breakout fantasy wideout, Watson checks seemingly every box. Talented player? Check. Fantasy-friendly offense? Yep. Vacated targets and routes? You bet. Good quarterback? I’d say so.

It’s time to roll.

The departure of both Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks is going to have a massive impact. Though Watson has demonstrated serious potential throughout his career, it has unfortunately been on limited volume. Since entering the NFL in 2022, Watson has averaged just 4.73 targets per game, while never eclipsing a 20% target share. The Fantasy Life projections have Watson penciled in for closer to seven targets per game this season, as Green Bay’s usual wide receiver rotation will be much, much tighter this year. Doubs led the Packers with a 77% route rate last season, while Wicks was just over 50%. But overall, five Green Bay receivers ran at least half of the routes. That is going to be very condensed this upcoming season, while Doubs’ absence in particular could really benefit Watson.

We love touchdowns in fantasy football, right? I thought so. Watson has scored 20 touchdowns on 133 career receptions (15%) and could be in line for the most red zone work of his career. Both Watson and Doubs entered the league in 2022. Since then, Watson ranks 20th among receivers in end zone targets (33), with Doubs right behind him (29). And once Watson made his debut this past season, he and Doubs actually tied for the team lead in end zone target share (33%). Doubs also accounted for 32% of the Packers' targets from inside the 10-yard line, the eighth-highest rate in football. So Watson has essentially been splitting end zone looks with Doubs, yet still has scored plenty of touchdowns. And now Doubs is gone?

Sign me up.

Overall, Watson’s role seems ready to expand. We already know that while Reed and Golden compete for snaps in two-wide sets, Watson will be a staple. Doubs led the team in routes from 12 personnel during the second half of last season, but Watson was right behind him. With both Doubs and Wicks gone, Watson will always be on the field in 12 personnel, a grouping Matt LaFleur deployed 20 plays per game a year ago, the sixth-most in football. It also looks like Watson’s usage is set to change in 2026. Watson appears to be playing more of the ‘Z’ receiver role this season, which means more movement and designed looks. Dwain McFarland highlighted Watson’s encouraging preseason usage in his Week 2 Preseason Takeaways article (an absolute must-read), pointing out that he was used quite a bit in motion and play-action passes, two fantasy cheat codes for wide receivers.

More creative usage would be a welcome sight for Watson, who ranks just 64th among receivers in routes from motion since 2022 (108). LaFleur’s offense should lean on motion, helping Watson get more free releases and layup looks. Since 2020, Green Bay’s ranks in shift-motion:

2020: 50% (5th)

2021: 54% (5th)

2022: 57% (8th)

2023: 61% (5th)

2024: 70% (3rd)

2025: 59% (8th)

We mentioned how the lack of volume has held Watson (and most Green Bay pass-catchers) back in fantasy over the years. Playing in a WR rotation already hurts your target and route upside, but it’s even more difficult in a run-first offense. Over the past three years, the Packers have sported the league’s fourth-lowest neutral script pass rate (53%), while Jordan Love ranks 17th in dropbacks per game during that span (33.3). Given Love’s efficiency, it would be fun to see what this offense could look like if he threw the football more.

But what if that’s this season?

This time last year, the Packers looked like one of the best defenses in all of football. And that carried over into the season. But everything changed in Week 15. Green Bay lost Micah Parsons to a torn ACL, and from that point on, this once vaunted defense suddenly became one to attack.

During the final four weeks of the year (including the playoffs), Green Bay’s defense fell apart. With Parsons off the field, the Packers posted a 3.7% sack rate, compared to 7.3% with Parsons on the field. And with Parsons sidelined for the final four weeks of the season, Green Bay allowed over 28 points per game. That resulted in the Packers' pass rate when leading by four-plus points climbing to 62%, the fifth-highest rate in football. For reference, from Weeks 1-15 with Parsons healthy, that pass rate was down at 52% (18th).

Entering the 2026 campaign, it appears the earliest possible date we could see Parsons return is Week 6, which means Green Bay’s passing rate might climb quite a bit during the first half of the season. And an uptick in potential targets for Watson is exciting. Again, we project Watson to average 6.7 targets per game this upcoming season. There have been 20 regular season games in Watson’s career where he’s seen at least six targets. In those games, Watson has averaged 66 receiving yards and 14.9 PPR PPG. For reference, 14.9 PR PPG would have been good for WR10 last season, albeit in a down year for the wide receiver position. That still would have been good for WR17 in 2024.

Should You Draft Christian Watson?

If he can stay healthy (yes, that is a concern), Watson legitimately has top-15 upside this season. Yet he’s still being drafted as the WR29 over on Underdog, and I’ve done drafts on other platforms where Watson has been a bench receiver.

Yes, please.

I understand some skeptics point to Watson’s injury track record, which is rather lengthy. ACL tear, ankle sprain, hamstring strains, knee bruise, etc. Some may see that resume and think “injury prone.” But every player in the NFL is injury prone.

Until they’re not.

My excitement in Watson’s talent and opportunity outweighs any potential injury concerns. And far too many times in fantasy, our “glass half empty” mindset wins. “What if Watson gets hurt?”

But what if he doesn’t? That’s something I’m excited to find out.

text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- Denver Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper was placed on the NFL's commissioner exempt list Sunday, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter.

It means Cooper, who is scheduled to be in Douglas County (Colo.) court Monday for arraignment on domestic violence charges, can neither practice nor play in games for the Broncos while he is on the list. The timing of the move means Cooper does not count against the 53 players on Denver's roster leading up to Sunday's cut deadline.

The list is designed to remove a player from participation in games and practices while potential violations of the NFL's personal conduct policy are reviewed. Cooper could still face a league suspension. He will be paid while on the exempt list and can work out in the Broncos' facility and attend meetings, but he cannot participate in on-field activities.

Cooper was arrested twice in a seven-day span in June on domestic violence charges relating to incidents involving his girlfriend. He faces a felony charge of second-degree assault by strangulation and three misdemeanors, including violating a protection order. A trial date could be set Monday at his arraignment if no settlement is reached in his case before the 1:30 p.m. MT court appearance.

While most of the Broncos were given the night off in Friday's preseason finale, Cooper played eight snaps in the game. After the Broncos' 34-6 victory over the Minnesota Vikings, coach Sean Payton said Cooper had played, at least in part, because of the uncertainty surrounding his availability to start the regular season.

"Part of it also was you have to look behind [him], like who's coming in for the next three-and-a-half quarters," Payton said. "So yes, he had good work."

The Broncos have elected to allow Cooper to participate throughout training camp practices and the preseason games, saying the team was "staying the course with the league protocol, with the club protocol, relative to what we've been advised to do."

The affidavit that was included in the police investigation into Cooper's first arrest June 4 included a report from the medical exam of Cooper's girlfriend. In it, a nurse wrote that the woman experienced a physical injury from being choked that led to a "substantial risk of death" or substantial risk of injury, including the possibility of traumatic brain injury.

Payton has consistently deferred to the NFL's investigation and the legal process when he has discussed the team's approach with the sixth-year linebacker. Payton said the Broncos set guidelines for Cooper after the arrest, and that has included therapy.

Cooper was a seventh-round pick in the 2021 draft and has 31.5 sacks in 81 career games with the Broncos, including eight sacks last season. He has started every game in each of the past three seasons.

text:
The NFL has placed Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper on the Commissioner Exempt List, a league spokesman confirmed to The Athletic. His placement on the list comes in the wake of two arrests resulting from domestic incidents with his then-girlfriend in June.

Cooper will be paid his full salary while on the exempt list, but he can’t play in games or practice with the team. He will be allowed to attend meetings and receive treatment at the team facility. Commissioner Roger Goodell has sole discretion to place a player on the list or remove them from it. The exemption is typically used for players who have pending legal cases and/or are still under investigation by the league.

The duration of time players spend on the exempt list has ranged from a few days to an entire season, and there’s no indication yet as to how long Cooper could remain on the list. He could still be subject to a suspension by the NFL.

Cooper will not count against the 53-man roster while he’s on the exempt list. The most likely player to take his spot in the starting lineup is Jonah Elliss, a third-year player selected in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft out of Utah. Elliss has 7.5 career sacks for the Broncos, including five during his rookie season. He missed four games last season due to injury.

Cooper’s absence will also mean a larger role for Que Robinson, a fourth-round pick out of Alabama last year who sacked New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye once in the AFC Championship Game. Robinson also had a sack in Denver’s second preseason game against the Green Bay Packers.

Cooper was initially arrested June 4 after police were called to his apartment following an altercation with his then-girlfriend. He was initially charged with domestic violence and misdemeanor criminal mischief. The charges were later upgraded to include felony second-degree assault by strangulation after a further review of the incident that included a report from a nurse who examined the woman the night of the initial incident. The nurse wrote in her report at the time that the woman suffered “serious bodily injury” that was consistent with “strangulation with hypoxia” and “traumatic brain injury,” according to an arrest affidavit.

Cooper was arrested a second time June 11 on a charge of violating a protection order put in place after the initial incident. He is due to appear for an arraignment hearing on Monday. He was excused from the Broncos’ minicamp in mid-June following the second arrest, but he reported to training camp along with the rest of the team on July 28 and has participated in every practice. He also started the first preseason game in Atlanta.

A seventh-round pick of the Broncos in 2021, Cooper finished second on the team last season with eight sacks. He had a career-high 10.5 sacks in 2024 and signed a four-year extension in November of that season that came with $33 million in guarantees.

text:
The Atlanta Falcons will try to shore up their defensive line with the acquisition of Gervon Dexter Sr. from the Chicago Bears on cut-down day.

The Falcons traded cornerback Clark Phillips III and a fifth-round draft pick to the Bears on Sunday morning for Dexter, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and Jeremy Fowler.

Dexter, 24, was a starter the last two seasons in Chicago, accumulating 11 sacks combined during that period. He was a second-round pick by the Bears in 2023.

New Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham was the assistant GM of the Bears when they selected Dexter, who is now in the final season of his rookie contract.

The Falcons struggled against the run last season and have made it a priority to improve the interior of their defensive line. They traded for Maason Smith and signed Da'Shawn Hand and Chris Williams in the offseason.

But Hand, who was expected to be an impact player, suffered a leg injury early in training camp and has not yet returned to practice. The 6-foot-6, 326-pound Dexter brings a big, physical presence to the position.

Dexter suffered a hamstring injury during Tuesday's practice, according to Bears coach Ben Johnson. He did not travel with the team to Tennessee for Chicago's joint practice and preseason finale Saturday night against the Titans.

Phillips, 24, was a fourth-round pick by the Falcons in 2023. He started seven games in 2023 and 2024 as mostly an outside corner, but missed most of last season with a triceps injury.

Chicago used ample resources to shore up its interior depth this offseason by signing free agents Neville Gallimore, Kentavius Street and James Lynch. The Bears' sole defensive line addition in the draft came in the sixth round, when they selected defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg from Georgia Tech.

The rookie earned high praise from coaches over the last six weeks as he worked his way into regular first-team reps.

"He's a beast," Johnson said of van den Berg. "This guy ... he's an incredible athlete. He's still learning the game of football to a degree, and yet it's amazing what he brings to the table."

ESPN's Courtney Cronin contributed to this report.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS – Running back Isiah Pacheco's status for the start of the regular season is up in the air because of a back injury. If Pacheco can't play Week 1 against the New Orleans Saints, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said he's "comfortable" with Jacob Saylors opening the year as Jahmyr Gibbs' backup.

"I am," Campbell said. "I’m comfortable with those guys. And I just like the thought of having a guy in our system, think that's important. Knows our terminology, knows our guys, knows the protections. Just kind of knows it all, man. Understands our quarterback and how he thinks. I just think that's important."

Saylors ran for 100 yards on 17 carries Saturday, Aug. 29, as the Lions closed the preseason with a 25-16 win over the Indianapolis Colts.

He had three runs of 16-plus yards Saturday and averaged 6 yards per carry for the preseason.

The Lions signed Pacheco to be Gibbs' primary backup after trading David Montogmery to Houston in the offseason, but Pacheco missed most of training camp with knee and back injuries.

Campbell said last week Pacheco's sprained knee had healed but the running back was "touch and go" with his back injury.

Gibbs is expected to shoulder the bulk of the work in the Lions backfield this fall, but he's never had more than 250 carries in a season.

Along with Saylors, the Lions are expected to keep Sione Vaki as a backup on their initial 53-man roster, and have Trayveon Williams and Jabari Small vying for roster spots. Small, who spent part of last season on the Lions' practice squad, left Saturday's game with an injury while Williams ran for 57 yards on nine carries.

Vaki did not play Saturday for precautionary reasons after missing the first two games of the preseason with a broken nose and back spasms.

"Small would kind of fall into that bucket just like Saylors would," Campbell said. "They’ve kind of got a feel of what we're doing and they've shown a little bit of stuff here that's good and they know our system. It doesn't mean we wouldn't go outside and see if something else is there, but I like those guys, and I like Saylors."

Saylors played primarily on special teams for the Lions last season after playing the 2024-25 spring seasons with the St. Louis Battlehawks of the UFL. He had two carries for 11 yards for the Lions last fall.

"He’s made plays out of the backfield.," Lions quarterback Josh Dobbs said. "He runs hard, he made plays. He’s hard to tackle. He’s very fast so I’m excited to see how we use him this year for sure."

text:
The NFL announced on Sunday that it has placed Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs on the Commissioner's Exempt List.

Jacobs is not permitted to practice or attend games while on the list.

The news comes as Jacobs faces misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property stemming from what police described as a physical confrontation with his girlfriend.

The formal charges, announced Thursday by Brown County (Wisc.) District Attorney David Lasee, stem from a May arrest in which he was initially booked on five counts, including felony strangulation.

“Josh Jacobs has been placed on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, which is an administrative procedure used by the NFL while a matter is being reviewed," Jacobs' lawyers, David Z. Chesnoff, Richard A. Schonfeld and Clarence F. Duchac III, said in a statement on Sunday, obtained by NFL Network Insider Ian Rapoport.

“It is not a final determination. Josh respects the NFL process, the Packers, and his coaches and teammates. He looks forward to his return to the team and the NFL.”

Jacobs attended and participated in the entirety of Green Bay's training camp outside of time he missed due to a groin injury.

Packers head coach Matt LaFleur told reporters on Friday following his team's final preseason game that he fully anticipated Jacobs "being a member of our team" but that he could not comment on Jacobs' potential availability for their regular-season opener against the Vikings on Sept. 13.

“I can’t really comment on that because I don’t know," LaFleur said on Friday.

Jacobs, 28, is entering his third campaign with the Packers, who signed him as a free agent in 2024.

The 24th overall pick of the 2019 NFL Draft by the Oakland Raiders, Jacobs is a three-time Pro Bowler with 7,803 career rushing yards and 74 rushing touchdowns. He led the NFL in rushing in 2022 with the Raiders.

Last season, Jacobs produced 929 yards and 13 touchdowns for Green Bay, which has Jacobs under contract through the 2027 season.

Through training camp, the WRs of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers have gotten pretty banged up. Their WR1, Emeka Egbuka, and WR3, Jalen McMillan, over the past month in the lead-up to the regular season, have picked up injury designations.

Egbuka got a toe injury in a joint practice against the New York Jets, and McMillan sustained a left knee injury in the midst of training camp.

Head Coach of Tampa Bay, Todd Bowles, recently commented on his two WRs, giving some insight into their availability for the Bucs' Week 1 matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals.

Jalen McMillan And Emeka Egbuka Injury Updates

Fox Sports beat writer for Tampa Bay, Greg Auman, said the following on X.

“Bowles said he expects Jalen McMillan and "hopefully" Emeka Egbuka to be ready for Week 1, doesn't think they'll need to carry an extra receiver on the 53 to offset short-term injuries.”

Those comments from Bowles are certainly encouraging for McMillan. But regarding Egbuka, fantasy owners should have slight concerns. He should not miss serious time, but it does seem like there is a possibility that he does not play in Week 1.

Jalen McMillan

Before McMillan had his minor knee injury, going into the 2026 season, injuries were already a major concern. In 2025, he only played in four games due to a major neck injury. That completely derailed the momentum he picked up as a fantasy prospect in the latter half of his rookie season of 2024.

In 2024, from Week 14 to Week 18, McMillan averaged 4.8 receptions and 63.2 receiving yards per game. Over that span, he also logged seven TDs and, in PPR fantasy formats, he was WR19.

Coming into 2026, he has one of the higher upsides as a fantasy player in his ADP range. In PPR formats in ESPN leagues, his ADP is WR60, and in Sleeper leagues, it is WR72.

Emeka Egbuka

Egbuka in year two has WR10 or better fantasy potential. That stems from him having a breakout rookie season—recording 63 receptions, 938 receiving yards, and six TDs–and also with longtime Tampa Bay WR1 Mike Evans now being on the San Francisco 49ers.

Egbuka did have a pretty poor close to the 2025 season. In his last eight games, he had over 50 receiving yards just one time. Also, over that stretch, he did not score a single touchdown. Despite that underwhelming run of production and even as just a second-year player, Egbuka should be the player Baker Mayfield leans on the most in Tampa Bay's pass game, as he is the most talented and dynamic WR that the Bucs currently have.`

Fantasy managers, even if Egbuka misses a couple of weeks, should still take him where his current ADP is. For PPR in ESPN leagues, Egbuka is WR19, and in Sleeper Leagues he is WR18. Last season in PPR, he finished as WR23. With the increased opportunity mentioned, with Evans being gone, that should be the lowest production level Egbuka has over his next several seasons in the NFL.

title: How it works: NFL Practice Squad rules, eligibility, salary, waiver wire, and more
description:
Practice squad players moving up to the main roster Like the last three seasons, teams have more flexibility with using practice squad players on game day.
Any practice squad player can be elevated and automatically reverts back to the practice squad after a game.
During the playoffs, practice squad players have unlimited elevations.
Practice squad basics Practice squad players practice with the team.
A practice squad player cannot be signed to another practice squad unless he is first released or waived.
text:
The Washington Commanders have to trim their roster down to 53 players by 6 p.m. ET today. The roster cuts will start before then, and many of those players will be signed to the team’s 17-man practice squad. Every team has to trim down from 90 or 91 players,

16 player squads

Practice squads were limited to 10 players in 2019, but that was set to change with the new CBA signed in 2020. The number was going to 12 players for 2 years, and then was going to be increased to 14 players in 2022. That all changed when the uncertainty of COVID-19 hit, and the league increased practice squads to 16 players, which will once again be the limit in 2026.

International Player Pathway Program

Teams participating in the International Player Pathway(IPP) program can have 91-man rosters during the offseason. They can also have a 17th practice squad member for the season, but if signed to the practice squad, that player can’t be signed to the regular season roster; however, starting in 2024 he can be elevated for up to three games. If the player is kept on the 53-man roster, he is subject to waiver rules.

The Washington Commanders currently have DE T.J. Maguranyanga on the roster, and he is eligible to be signed to their practice squad as the 17th member if he is waived and clears waivers. He is unlikely to be part of the 53-man roster.

Practice squad players moving up to the main roster

Like the last three seasons, teams have more flexibility with using practice squad players on game day. PS players can be activated on game day before the team announces their inactives (90 minutes before game time). Teams are allowed to elevate players from their practice squad to the game day roster without having to cut a member of the 53-man team. Accordingly, clubs can increase from the standard 53 to 55 players while game day active squads expand from a previous 46 to 47 players (or 48 if a team carries eight offensive linemen). Any practice squad player can be elevated and automatically reverts back to the practice squad after a game.

Each practice squad player is now able to be elevated up to three times per season. To be activated a fourth time requires the player to be signed to the regular roster. During the playoffs, practice squad players have unlimited elevations. This makes it easier for teams to have players they know and trust on game day, and also not have to subject them to waivers when they are signed to the main roster and cut to get back to the practice squad as was true in the past.

Veteran players

Another change is the eligibility requirements for veteran players. Previously teams could have up to 4 players who had two years of NFL experience. Now teams can have 6 veterans with no limit on the amount of accrued seasons they have in the league. A player must have been on full-play status for at least six regular-season games in a given season to gain an accrued season. This includes being on the active/inactive list, injured reserve or reserve PUP.

Weekly payment

Practice squad players make $13,750 per week or $247,500 for 18 weeks. Veteran players with over two years of experience make a minimum of $18,350 per week or $330,300 for 18 weeks, and a maximum of $22,8590 per week or $411,300 for 18 weeks.

Signing with the practice squad

Teams must complete their roster cuts by Sunday August 30th at 6 p.m. ET, meaning that almost 1,200 players will be released or placed on an injury list.

Teams have until Monday at noon to claim unvested players that have been waived.

Vested veterans (players with a minimum of 4 accrued seasons) become free agents immediately and are able to sign with any team.

Starting at 12:00 p.m. ET on August 31st, teams can begin signing players to their practice squads.

Practice squad basics

Practice squad players practice with the team. They do not play in games, unless they are elevated (see above)

Practice squad players are paid per week and can be released at any point during the season.

Practice squad players are free to sign with other NFL teams, but they have to be signed to the 53-man active roster of the acquiring team. A practice squad player cannot be signed to another practice squad unless he is first released or waived.

A practice squad player cannot sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game, or 10 days if his team is currently on a bye week.

If a practice squad player is signed to the active roster, he will receive a minimum of three weekly paychecks, even if he is released before spending three weeks with the new team.

In order to be signed to a practice squad after being released, a player who is not a vested veteran must first clear waivers, and is subject to waiver claims by other teams.

Waiver wire

The Washington Commanders had the No. 7 overall pick in this year’s draft, which means they have six teams in front of them that could potentially claim a player Washington wants. There should be plenty of players available, and Washington will be on the look out for some offensive line help next week.

The waiver order goes by original draft order not counting trades.

Teams maintain their places on the waiver priority list through Week 3 of the regular season.

After Week 3 the waiver priority order is determined by reverse order of wins.

Teams don’t lose their spot on the priority list like in fantasy football.

Teams can put in as many waiver claims as they want, and will be awarded the player(s) if they are the highest-ranked claiming team. Any player added through waivers will need a corresponding roster move to make room for him on the roster.

The claiming team picks up the player’s contract, not including any signing bonuses that his original team already paid.

Vested veterans (on an NFL roster for at least 6 games per season, for at least 4 seasons) aren’t subject to waivers until after the trade deadline, which will be after Week 9 this season.

Players who are waived/injured, and not claimed on waivers, return to their team and are placed on injured reserve unless an injury settlement is made.

There aren't many good options. We could keep all four, likely for just a few days, the way they did two years ago. Or there's a harder choice, to let Dillon Gabriel go, which is real tough to do because of what he showed on Thursday. They can both play. If Gabriel goes and becomes solid, it's not a good look for a team that has struggled to find capable quarterbacks for more than 30 years. It would be career-damaging for the guys in charge if Gabriel goes elsewhere and plays even remotely as well as he did on Thursday. Trying to sneak Green to the practice squad is a non-starter - too risky.

I have faith in Andrew Berry. It's a good thing I do, because no option looks perfect and most of them look bad.

THE LEAN: Two weeks ago, Austin Barber was a swing tackle. Now Todd Monken is leaving the right guard job open. Petrak had it Saturday. Cleveland.com had the PFF card: highest-graded Browns lineman in the preseason, highest in each of the last two games, which he started at guard with the twos. Teven Jenkins still has "the lean." Monken said it is not done. They have today and a few practices. Jacksonville is September 13.

Barber is 6-7, 320, picked in the third round from Florida. He had never played guard. They moved him inside because they wanted a look. Monken was pleasantly surprised he did not look out of place. The coaching tell was a screen. Casual the first time. The next week he ran through the defender. Tytus Howard called him a baller and said he can play everything but center. If he starts, you have two rookies on the line alongside Spencer Fano. Monken does not care. "Would it be ideal to have 11 rookies starting? Of course not." Put the best five out there. If that is Austin, great. If it is Teven, great.

All I can tell you is that some people whose football IQ I really respect just rave about him. It looks like the Browns' inquisitiveness about him at the guard position may pay dividends.

Berry traded up to get him. Day 2, after they had already traded back. You do not climb to 86 for a guy you plan to bury on the swing. You climb because tackles who can live inside are hard to find once the draft ends. Joel Bitonio used to be a tackle too. I am not putting Barber in Canton. I am saying the building just found out the kid they paid up for might be a starter in two weeks, and Monken is not pretending that is settled.

text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers concluded their 2026 preseason slate on Friday evening with a 19-0 loss in Jacksonville. That means the next time they take the field it will count as the regular season begins.

That won't happen immediately. Since paring its preseason down to three weeks in 2021, the NFL has had an extra week in the schedule between the final exhibition contest and the first set of regular-season games. The Buccaneers and all other NFL squads will use the next week to get their 53-man rosters and 16-man practice squads in shape before Week One begins. Once that happens, the Buccaneers will be ticketed for an opener in Cincinnati on Sunday, September 13 to take on Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, Dexter Lawrence and the Bengals. Kickoff is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET at Paycor Stadium.

The Buccaneers will be looking for a 1-0 start to their regular season for the sixth year in a row, but it will be against a Cincinnati team that boasts a high-powered offense and is hoping for much better defensive results after the offseason trade for Lawrence and the free agency additions of safety Bryan Cook and edge rusher Boye Mafe. Since going to the Super Bowl in the 2021 season and the AFC Championship game in 2022, the Bengals have missed the playoffs for three straight years, but that has largely been due to injuries to Burrow and a cratering defense.

When healthy, Burrow is clearly one of the most productive quarterbacks in the NFL. He played all 17 games in 2024 and led the NFL with 4,918 passing yards and 43 touchdown passes. He is surrounded with elite playmaking talent in Chase (6,837 receiving yards and 54 touchdowns in five seasons), fellow wideout Tee Higgins and running back Chase Brown. The Buccaneers will hope that their efforts to significantly amplify their edge rush rotation have paid off, giving them a chance to disrupt Burrow's timing.

After the additions of Lawrence and Mafe, the Bengals appear to have a more dangerous defensive front of their own, also now featuring defensive tackle Jonathan Allen and second-round edge rusher Cashius Howell. The Bucs will counter with an offensive line that, after a severely injury-plagued 2025 season, is back to the starting five that produced very impressive results in 2024, anchored by All-Pro left tackle Tristan Wirfs. The Bucs will also be unveiling a new offensive coordinated by Zac Robinson and now featuring a stacked receiver room and a new running back tandem with Kenny Gainwell joining Bucky Irving.

The Buccaneers won four straight NFC South titles from 2021-24, and that was after capturing the Super Bowl LV title in 2020, but they missed the playoffs last season on a tiebreaker. The team is aiming to get back into title contention in 2025, and it starts in Cincinnati.

title: Yankees hopeful George Lombard Jr. can avoid IL; Red Sox season series finale looms

text:
NEW YORK — Aaron Boone was peeved by his team’s performance in a matinee loss in Saturday’s doubleheader at Yankee Stadium. Then George Lombard Jr., the shortstop who had played every inning of his brief New York Yankees career, twisted his right knee early in the second game.

“Good enough to stay in right now,” Boone, the Yankees’ manager, told Ken Rosenthal on Fox as the top of the third inning began, but he didn’t sound hopeful. The next pitch sailed over the right field fence for a Boston Red Sox homer. The day was becoming a disaster.

But while Lombard was visiting New York-Presbyterian Hospital in the middle innings, the Yankees (77-59) recovered to wallop the Red Sox, 9-2, and earn a split. They now lead Boston (74-62) by three games for the top American League wild-card spot.

Lombard might not play on Sunday, when the winner will clinch the season series and a potential tiebreaker between the teams. But the Yankees believe Lombard will avoid the injured list, even without definitive word on his test results.

“They’re still waiting to make sure and clarify, but it looks like a day-to-day situation,” Boone said postgame.

Lombard was batting against Brayan Bello in the second when he twisted his knee while rotating his hips on a fastball that veered inside. The ball did not hit Lombard, but he asked for time after the awkward movement.

He grimaced and hopped out of the box on his left foot, then grabbed at his knee and flexed it with a trainer before staying in and singling to left on the next pitch.

“A little weird discomfort,” Boone described it after the game. “He was going to swing and then kind of really shut down. I think he caught his spike a little bit as he was kind of putting the brakes on. Just kind of tweaked it.”

Lombard played defense in the top of the third and batted again in the bottom of the inning, flying out to left. But Boone removed him before the top of the fourth, shifting José Caballero to shortstop and bringing in Amed Rosario to play third base.

“I heard that it’s not too bad,” Caballero said. “It’s great news because he’s been playing really well. So we need the whole group together and healthy.”

Lombard, 21, has become integral to the group since arriving on Aug. 4, after the Yankees refused to trade him at the deadline. He is hitting .253/.310/.367 with two home runs in 23 games, though he has committed seven errors.

His single was part of an unusual attack by the Yankees, who had 13 singles without an extra-base hit in Saturday’s second game. The last time they did that in a nine-inning game (per a Stathead search) was May 1, 1999, in Kansas City. Chuck Knoblauch had three hits that night; Luis García Jr. did it this time.

García, acquired from the Washington Nationals in a trade on Aug. 3, has 15 hits (including four homers) in his last 10 games. He is hitting .309 for the Yankees and will not be a free agent until after the 2027 season.

“You’re seeing a guy (at) 26 years old really come of age this year, and he hasn’t really missed the beat since coming over to us,” Boone said. “We’re thrilled to have him because he’s a dangerous, dangerous hitter.”

The Yankees haven’t had enough of those in their summer without Aaron Judge, who has not played since May 31 because of a stress fracture of his right rib. In 75 games without Judge before Saturday, the Yankees had a .220 average and a .290 on-base percentage, both MLB lows, and had outscored only the Seattle Mariners during that time.

The first game brought more futility, with the Yankees looking all but helpless in a 6-0 loss to Jake Bennett and three relievers. Their Game 2 outburst came mostly with an eighth-inning singles parade off Raymond Burgos, Boston’s extra man for the doubleheader.

The Yankees’ best news was probably the return of Max Fried, who missed two weeks with a recurrence of a left elbow bone bruise. Fried was on a pitch count and still hasn’t earned a victory since April, but he said he felt strong for 3 ⅔ innings, striking out four and allowing one run.

“I would say I was feeling really strong before this IL stint, and I was feeling good in the (Aug. 14) game, it was just one little pitch that irritated it,” Fried said. “So to be able to get through, feel really good and come out healthy, that’s all I can ask for.”

Lombard will be back at Yankee Stadium on Sunday with an update on his status. If he can say something similar after Saturday’s scare, that is all the Yankees can ask for, too.

title: Parents should think twice about letting their kids play tackle football - MS NOW
authors: Anthony L. Fisher, Jason Page, Keith Reed, Kevin B. Blackistone
description:
On Tuesday, yet another study linking the repetitive head trauma experienced by NFL players to chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, later in life was released.
The New York Times reported on research published in the British Medical Journal examining CTE among former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021.
But researchers cannot say 91.4% of NFL players develop CTE because those brains weren’t a random sample.

text:
On Tuesday, yet another study linking the repetitive head trauma experienced by NFL players to chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, later in life was released.

The New York Times reported on research published in the British Medical Journal examining CTE among former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021. Of 878 former players who died during that period, 235 had their brains examined. Of those, 215 were diagnosed with CTE.

That’s 91.4%.

But researchers cannot say 91.4% of NFL players develop CTE because those brains weren’t a random sample. Even if every one of the other 643 players whose brains weren’t examined did not have CTE, those 215 confirmed cases still represent 24.5% of the entire group.

At least 1 in 4.

As usual, the NFL’s media partners at ESPN were largely silent. “Get Up” host Mike Greenberg spent 55 seconds reading the findings from a teleprompter. “First Take” similarly devoted 43 seconds to it. The network’s highest-paid star commentator, Pat McAfee, didn’t touch the story at all.

But this isn’t another column arguing that the NFL isn’t doing enough to protect its players, nor am I suggesting we abolish professional or college football. I think the NFL is doing about as much as it reasonably can to make an inherently violent sport safer when its athletes are bigger, stronger and faster than ever.

College and NFL players are adults. They know the risks. If they decide those risks are worth taking, that’s their choice.

My concern is with those who cannot meaningfully make that choice for themselves.

Children.

Roughly two million American kids under 18 play tackle football each year. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found an average of about 53,700 emergency-department visits annually for football-related traumatic brain injuries among children.

And those are just the injuries serious enough to reach an emergency room.

What about the concussion that never gets diagnosed? Or the kid who “gets his bell rung,” sits out a couple of plays and goes back into the game? More importantly, what about the hundreds of ordinary hits a child can absorb during a season that never produce concussion symptoms at all?

That’s increasingly where the CTE conversation is headed: not simply diagnosed concussions, but the cumulative effect of repetitive head impacts.

It’s one thing if an adult wants to roll the dice with his future health. And let’s be honest, it’s a gamble worth considering when you look at the money being handed out in college football and the NFL. We’re talking about life-changing and, in some cases, generational wealth.

An adult can weigh the potential reward against the potential consequences. A 12-year-old cannot.

More articles

A child — whose father hopes to live out his football dreams vicariously through his son — doesn’t possess that same depth of knowledge. He cannot meaningfully consent to the potential long-term consequences of repeatedly subjecting his developing brain to violent collisions.

Children need to be protected, even if they want to play.

So how do we do it without eliminating the game?

Perhaps tackle football shouldn’t begin until age 10 or 12. Flag football could replace it before then, eliminating years of unnecessary collisions. We could dramatically reduce or eliminate full-contact tackling in practice. We could ban high-impact collision drills. We could require independent medical professionals at games. We could also examine matching younger players by size and physical development, rather than simply age, so a 90-pound child isn’t routinely colliding with someone twice his size.

None of these ideas alone ultimately solve the problem, and there is no uniform national standard. Different leagues, organizations and states operate under different rules.

So football season begins again around the country. Games will be played. Teams will win and teams will lose. Millions of us will watch because football remains an incredible game.

I’m certainly going to watch.

But the more we learn about what repeated blows to the head can do to the human brain, the harder it becomes to pretend we don’t know there’s a cost.

Adults can decide whether that cost is worth paying.

Children cannot.

And if we aren’t willing to stop them from playing tackle football, we owe it to them to make sure they aren’t paying a price decades from now for a decision they weren’t old enough to understand.

Dillon Gabriel's stellar performance in the Cleveland Browns' preseason finale was enough to earn him a spot on their 53-man roster.

The Browns will be keeping the second-year quarterback entering the regular season, ESPN reported Sunday.

Gabriel joins Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders as the other quarterbacks on Cleveland's roster.

title: Steelers Land In Bottom Half Of CBS Sports' NFL Roster Rankings
description:
While a lot can change once the season kicks off, Pittsburgh’s roster doesn’t appear to have any major holes.
Jamel Dean, Jaquan Brisker, and Rayshawn Jenkins all provide options in a secondary that was challenged a year ago.
But where does the Steelers’ roster rank in the larger NFL landscape?
Jordan Dajani and Tyler Sullivan ranked all 32 NFL rosters and had Pittsburgh at No.
The injury concerns are real at safety, but it isn’t the only reason Dajani and Sullivan docked Pittsburgh’s roster in their rankings.
text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers had a busy offseason. With 10 draft picks and a slew of veterans brought in via free agency and trade, there are plenty of new faces on this year’s roster.

While a lot can change once the season kicks off, Pittsburgh’s roster doesn’t appear to have any major holes. Michael Pittman Jr. and Germie Bernard were brought in to shore up a wide receiver room that was lacking. Jamel Dean, Jaquan Brisker, and Rayshawn Jenkins all provide options in a secondary that was challenged a year ago.

But where does the Steelers’ roster rank in the larger NFL landscape? According to CBS Sports, it’s in the bottom half of the league. Jordan Dajani and Tyler Sullivan ranked all 32 NFL rosters and had Pittsburgh at No. 19, with their main questions being at two positions.

At safety, the question is less about the players’ ability but more about their ability to stay on the field.

“There are some durability concerns with this group. Pittsburgh inked Jaquan Brisker to a one-year deal in free agency, and while he played in all 17 games for Chicago last season and broke up eight passes, he has a history of concussions,” Dajani and Sullivan wrote. “Meanwhile, DeShon Elliott was limited to five games last year due to injury. To compound the concern surrounding their injury history is the lack of depth behind them.”

Brisker has missed the entire preseason with an injury and his status is unclear as the regular season nears. Elliott is healthy after missing the second half of last season due to injury and will return to his starting role, but who will start beside him if Brisker remains out is unclear.

Jenkins has played well in preseason action as a late addition to the roster but is not guaranteed to make the team. Robert Spears-Jennings has impressed as well, but likely can’t be trusted as a starter as a seventh-round rookie.

Jalen Ramsey, who has battled injury himself since training camp, is another option at safety, but Pittsburgh would prefer to use him as a chess piece that moves around the defense.

The injury concerns are real at safety, but it isn’t the only reason Dajani and Sullivan docked Pittsburgh’s roster in their rankings. They also pointed to the quarterback position.

“Aaron Rodgers already announced this season as his last, and it stands to wonder what Pittsburgh will get out of the 42-year-old,” Dajani and Sullivan write. “While his 24-7 touchdown-to-interception ratio was inside the top 10 in 2025, Rodgers’ numbers beyond that were middling. He was 16th among 33 qualified QBs in completion percentage, 15th in passing yards and 27th in yards per attempt. Does that improve, decline, or stay the same in 2026?”

Pittsburgh’s best hope is that added weapons on offense and a new, offensive-minded head coach who has a history with Rodgers is enough to see an improved Rodgers in 2026. Given the weight of the position, and what we saw from Rodgers last season, it’s fair to negatively impact Pittsburgh’s ranking based on not having one of the league’s best signal callers.

title: Jacob Thomas' Injury Shouldn't Stop Him From Making Vikings' 53-Man Roster
description:
There was a scary moment early in the third and final preseason game for the Minnesota Vikings on Friday night.
Against the Denver Broncos, undrafted free agent safety Jacob Thomas went down with what appeared to be a leg injury, and fans immediately expected the worst.
Why Jacob Thomas' injury won't hurt his chances to make the 53-man roster Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell stated after the game that he believed Thomas' injury was an ankle sprain, but the team wouldn't know for sure until an MRI was completed to evaluate the severity of the damage.
Now that the preseason is over for the Vikings, Thomas has until Sept. 13 to rest up.
With the positive news of his ankle injury, Thomas should be a member of the purple and gold when the border battle goes down in Week 1.
text:
There was a scary moment early in the third and final preseason game for the Minnesota Vikings on Friday night. Against the Denver Broncos, undrafted free agent safety Jacob Thomas went down with what appeared to be a leg injury, and fans immediately expected the worst.

Thomas has been a solid player during training camp and has put together a good preseason. Against the New York Giants in the preseason opener, he had four tackles (two solo) and one pass defense.

He followed that up with another good game against the Baltimore Ravens last weekend, where he was tied for the most tackles among all Vikings defenders, registering six takedowns (four solo) and adding one pass breakup.

Seeing him go down against the Broncos on Friday night seemed devastating to the 22-year-old defender from James Madison University. That said, the timing couldn't have been worse with the deadline to trim rosters to 53-players on the horizon.

Why Jacob Thomas' injury won't hurt his chances to make the 53-man roster

Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell stated after the game that he believed Thomas' injury was an ankle sprain, but the team wouldn't know for sure until an MRI was completed to evaluate the severity of the damage.

It turns out that O'Connell knew what he was talking about. On Saturday, Alec Lewis of The Athletic shared on X that the injury was a Grade 1 ankle sprain, which should be considered great news considering how bad it could have been.

Thomas' success during training camp and the preseason was one of the best stories to come out of the team.

In college, he played 50 games over four seasons, racking up 199 total tackles, 13 tackles for loss, five interceptions, and two sacks. With that kind of stat line in college, it isn't shocking that he thrived early with Minnesota.

The six-foot-one, 212-pound defensive back was on track to make the team's 53-man roster this season, and this injury shouldn't stop that from happening. While he will need some time to recover, this ankle injury isn't severe enough to place him on injured reserve or persuade the team to add a different safety in his place.

When looking at the safety room for Minnesota, the lack of depth behind Josh Metellus and Theo Jackson is highly concerning. Keeping a physical player with a great nose for the football who can play close to the line of scrimmage or drop back into coverage would be a huge asset in Brian Flores' defense.

Therefore, parting ways with him due to this injury would be foolish for the Vikings since they won't find someone with his skill set and physical attributes in free agency during roster cuts, and he has outplayed the other safeties fighting for a roster spot during his time in Minnesota.

Now that the preseason is over for the Vikings, Thomas has until Sept. 13 to rest up. That is when Minnesota will host the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium to open the regular season. With the positive news of his ankle injury, Thomas should be a member of the purple and gold when the border battle goes down in Week 1.

In other words, the more space and time between shell contact and head contact, the better—similar to car crash safety techniques.

There’s a reason why Patrick Mahomes’s helmet looks like that. The nearly $700 piece of headgear protecting the Kansas City Chiefs star quarterback sits high atop his dome in part because of a crowning discovery from decades of testing: Distance makes the head blow softer.

In other words, the more space and time between shell contact and head contact, the better—similar to car crash safety techniques. That’s why today’s helmets are bigger and less rigid than their predecessors. Inside, 3D-printed, collapsible liners compress better than foam to absorb more impact.

Modern progress happened quickly:

“We’ve seen more change in roughly the last 14 years than we probably did in the previous 40,” the director of the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab—the leading authority in football helmet safety—told the publication Science.

text:
Bears rookie wide receiver Zavion Thomas missed the first two preseason games with a knee injury. When he finally got on the field on Saturday, he put on a show.

Thomas caught a pass from Tyson Bagent and raced 97 yards to the end zone on his very first NFL play, and finished his first preseason game with five catches for 140 yards, plus a 31-yard punt return and a 22-yard kickoff return.

Asked if anyone had a chance of catching him on his long touchdown, the speedy Thomas said he didn’t know which Titans player was chasing him, but answered, “Nah, he didn’t have a chance.”

Thomas said that even while he couldn’t practice because of his knee, older players were helping him prepare for the moment when he would be on the field, so he expected to play well once he got medical clearance.

“It felt amazing. The preparation put into it, it was something that I expected,” Thomas said.

Thomas didn’t put up big numbers during his four years of college football (two at Mississippi State and two at LSU), but he put up an eye-popping number at the Scouting Combine: 4.28 seconds in the 40-yard dash. That got him plenty of attention, and the Bears took a chance on him in the third round.

Bagent knows Thomas’s speed is a huge asset to the Bears’ offense.

“Give Zavion a chance and then you’re able to see that speed, which is a big reason why he’s here,” Bagent said. “I think that was Zavion Thomas’s first play in the NFL, so greatest start in NFL history.”

title: NFL preseason Week 3 takeaways: Fernando Mendoza ready, Anthony Richardson improved
description:
The third-and-final week of preseason action, which concluded Saturday, featured a host of players hoping to nudge difficult decisions in their favor.
Mendoza’s final preseason stat line wasn’t pretty, but he’s ahead of where I thought he’d be.
If the offensive line improves and the playoffs look like they’re out of reach, Mendoza is absolutely ready to take over.

text:
The Athletic has live coverage of the NFL’s roster cut deadline.

It’s a wonder how we ever got through four weeks of preseason games. Three is the perfect number.

The third-and-final week of preseason action, which concluded Saturday, featured a host of players hoping to nudge difficult decisions in their favor. But that’s not all. We also saw that Fernando Mendoza’s stats don’t reflect how good he’s been, that Anthony Richardson Sr. is looking right at home in Indianapolis, and that Green Bay could benefit down the road by letting Jordan Love call a few plays. Here are some takeaways at the close of preseason action.

Raiders are right to start Cousins, though Mendoza is ready

All signs point to the Las Vegas Raiders naming Kirk Cousins as their starting quarterback, which was the plan all along. Mendoza’s final preseason stat line wasn’t pretty, but he’s ahead of where I thought he’d be. He is comfortable under center, and his footwork and ability to get through multiple reads have looked smooth. There are certainly plays he would like to have back, and his pocket movements could at times be better. On a pick-six against the Houston Texans, he drifted to the left, which caused his running back to drift that way and led to a miscommunication.

His interception against the San Francisco 49ers was a high pass thrown over the middle of the field. The play was a play-action “drift” concept. After the play-fake, 49ers linebacker Jalen Graham did a great job of getting back into his zone. Mendoza successfully threw the ball over Graham, but receiver Jalen Nailor had to fully extend in the middle of the field to try to catch it. Nailor dropped the pass, and it was intercepted.

“I thought that was an excellent throw,” Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said after reviewing the film. “He ripped it, just like we asked him to, on time. Yeah, it was a little bit high. Jalen’s gotta make a play.”

Coaches from this tree (Shanahan/Kubiak/McVay) want their quarterbacks to attempt these types of throws without hesitation. Jimmy Garoppolo and Brock Purdy have thrown these passes throughout their careers, but their arms are a lot weaker than Mendoza’s. Hopefully, the Raiders find a bigger target for Mendoza to attempt such audacious throws.

Mendoza has shown enough of a mental baseline to play, and he’ll improve with reps. But starting Cousins is the right move. The Raiders must find out how much the offensive line has progressed from the bottom-tier unit it was last season. Putting Mendoza in a situation where he has to run for his life would be bad for his development. If the offensive line improves and the playoffs look like they’re out of reach, Mendoza is absolutely ready to take over.

Tagovailoa, Penix Jr. or … Jack Strand?

Tua Tagovailoa had a golden opportunity to establish himself as the Atlanta Falcons’ starting quarterback, but after shaky performances in joint practices and botching two snaps in 25 preseason reps, he’s opened the door for Michael Penix Jr. to overtake him, even though Penix didn’t play at all in the preseason.

But Penix doesn’t seem like a great fit for coach Kevin Stefanski’s system. He isn’t comfortable turning his back to the defense on play-action concepts and hasn’t liked throwing into the middle since college. Would the Falcons consider giving UDFA quarterback Jack Strand a start if Penix falters when he gets his shot?

Strand is close to 6 feet, 4 inches tall and 240 pounds. He has a sidearm whip release, but throws with zip and accuracy. He’s also a threat as a runner. Strand is coming from Minnesota State-Moorhead, a Division II school, but he looks to have at least earned a roster spot.

If Penix wins the job, he’ll have a long leash and every opportunity as a first-round pick. But he needs to be much better than he’s been so far as a pro. If Penix can’t do it and Strand continues to improve behind the scenes, why shouldn’t he get a shot in a potential gap year for the Falcons?

Richardson is where he belongs

After a tumultuous period with Indianapolis, a stretch that included his benching in favor of Daniel Jones, a serious eye injury, a trade request, and a possible demotion to third string, it looks like Anthony Richardson Sr. has settled in with the Colts. Richardson looked as good as I’ve ever seen him in the first preseason game against the Patriots. His footwork and mechanics have looked more efficient and, as a result, his accuracy has improved. He was comfortable playing from the pocket and still has the freaky athleticism to make plays when things break down. In Week 2, the Colts gave Riley Leonard a shot at starting. Richardson had to play with the third team, which didn’t give him much help in making an impression.

But in the final preseason game against the Lions, when he had one drive with some starters and two with the backups, Richardson looked in control and accurate again. He had one miscommunication on a fade route to Laquon Treadwell but threw accurately overall, finishing 7-for-10 for 80 yards.

The best scenario for Richardson was always to stay with the Colts. No system in the league fits his skill set better, and he would need time to learn another system. Richardson is still just 24 and is immensely talented. With Jones’ injury history, there will always be a chance the Colts will have to go back to Richardson. If that time comes, he has to be ready to take advantage of it after such a productive offseason.

Jordan Love, offensive coordinator

Green Bay head coach Matt LaFleur said he let Jordan Love call plays in the second half of the Packers’ 42-38 comeback win against the Cardinals. His play calling led to 18 points and helped the Packers erase an 11-point fourth-quarter deficit. On a third-and-21 in the third quarter, when most offensive coordinators would call a screen or draw to get to the next series, Love called a deep shot, and it almost worked. Receiver Isaiah Neyor was open, and QB Kyle McCord threw a perfect ball that went through Neyor’s hands.

Though this was a fun exercise for the Packers, I thought it was smart and could ultimately benefit both Love and LaFleur. Love got to experience what LaFleur has to think about in different situations and how to set up plays. He got a peek into the why of each play call. Sometimes, quarterbacks can call plays during two-minute drills. Love got to experience that on the sideline with the Packers down by 11 points. He caught the Cardinals in man coverage with a perfect deep-shot call, which led to a 28-yard touchdown pass from McCord to Kisean Johnson.

Then, when the Packers got the ball back in their territory down by four, he got to experience play calling with the Packers wanting to score but also wanting to bleed the clock. This experience should help Love understand what LaFleur is thinking about in similar situations and will help him when he has to call or change a play. Play-calling head coaches often let other assistant coaches call plays in the preseason, but letting a young quarterback do so seems beneficial.

The great center shortage

There is a center shortage in the NFL. Last season, Frank Ragnow’s retirement and failed comeback attempt devastated the Lions’ offensive line. This offseason, former Bears center Drew Dalman suddenly retired, and fellow centers Cade Mays (Lions), Tyler Biadasz (Chargers) and Danny Pinter (Ravens) were injured.

Multiple teams are looking for center depth, including the Vikings, Jets and Commanders. I just watched Colts backup center Dalton Tucker have one of the worst games I’ve ever seen as far as inaccurate shotgun snaps. Finding a quality center is as important as ever with the proliferation of the Shanahan/McVay system. Teams will be scouring the waiver wire for them over the next couple of weeks.

text:
A GRIP ON SPORTS • As far back as I can remember, Sundays have been lazy days. The calm after Saturday’s storms. The deep breath before Monday’s hamster wheel rolls again. A day for quiet contemplation of whatever higher power guides you. Until kickoff.

•••••••

• Ya, NFL Sundays are different. Not sure if they are better or worse than the other 30 or so Sundays, but they are different. And, honestly? It’s about gosh-darn time they arrived.

Why is it in the 21st Century, the NFL still has to take this winding, waste-of-our time to get the season started? A month of camp? Three glorified scrimmages? Nothing on Labor Day weekend?

Let’s get it started already.

• Of course I have been asked to do a few things around the homestead today. And there is no NFL to distract the woman with a 12s T-shirt in her closet. Sadly, I just realized there won’t be any NFL games that matter, to her, on a Sunday until Sept. 20. As defending Super Bowl champions, the Seahawks open the year on a Wednesday. At home against New England. Then have 11 days before they are in Arizona, their personal house of (injury) horrors.

There’s a lot of yard work that can get done between now and then.

• There will be some NFL news today. It’s roster-announcement day, when each team must whittle their depth to the nub and decide on their top 53 players. Who will the Hawks pick? There are guesses out there. Lots of them. Always one more than you might think.

All of them, though, are moot by 3 p.m. Funny thing, though. So is the initial roster not too long after. There are often waiver claims made. And more cuts. Positions of need – everyone has one or two – are bolstered and depth at others are shaved a bit. Plus, the practice squad dance begins for those players cut and are available to other teams through waivers.

• Not a good opening weekend for the local Big Sky schools. And by local, I am referring to those west of Lookout Pass, though first-year Montana head coach Bobby Kennedy came really close to having to relocate after just one game.

Idaho couldn’t hold a late lead Friday night at Cal Poly, yielding a fourth-down touchdown pass with 8 seconds left in a 38-34 defeat. Those type of losses can be crushing.

Or is it worse to race out to a 24-3 lead on the road against the 25th-ranked team in the nation – and then score three more points in the final 33 minutes to lose 34-27? That was Eastern Washington’s fate Saturday in Flagstaff. That three-touchdown lead came with less than 3 minutes before halftime. And right before the Lumberjacks returned the ensuing kickoff for their first touchdown.

Another one before half gave NAU momentum, it rode that horse to a 27-24 fourth-quarter lead, Eastern tied it 10 minutes left and the Lumberjacks’ Ty Pennington, one of the best the Big Sky’s best quarterbacks led the game-winOKning touchdown drive in the waning moments.

• Oh, ya. The Mariners lost again Saturday. Kade Anderson was just fine. The bullpen and the defense’s situational awareness were not. And, wow, did Eduard Bazardo look silly.

Last season ended in Toronto. If it weren’t for the American League West ineptitude, so would any hopes for this one.

Here are the division’s current streaks, from top to bottom: lost one, lost four, lost three, lost two, lost six. And their seasonal run differential: -46, -54, -65, -188, -79. The teams are, in order, Astros, Rangers, M’s, A’s and Angels.

What a motley crew.

• One week to the Apple Cup. Plan accordingly. That’s it. That’s the note.

• It’s been an awful weekend around these parts. So much so, I made sure to take a quick peek a Kim’s daily aphorism from Ram Dass before getting started this morning.

Under a picture of two children walking away from the camera, down a wooded path are the words “We’re all just walking each other home.”

Worth remembering on a Sunday morning. And every morning.

•••

WSU: The Cougars’ receiving corps is better when Branden Ganashamoorthy is healthy. At least faster. But, yes, better too. Greg Woods takes us down his path back from the broken ankle he suffered during spring practices. … We mentioned the Apple Cup above in passing. Jon Wilner mentions it too in today’s Mercury News. In a lot more than passing. Though, in fact, once this contract runs out, the rivalry might just pass into the realm of once was. … Elsewhere in the Pac-12, Wilner’s mailbag we passed along yesterday? It is on the S-R site today. … John Canzano was happy to see games on a Saturday. … New Oregon State athletic director Kevin Griffin wants the Beavers to move on from the past two years. And only look ahead. … We love reading stories about Boise State’s running backs as their position coach played at WSU while we were covering the Cougs. … Could Fresno State upset USC and use that to slingshot into a CFP berth? … In basketball news, this CBS Sports story should scare everyone. … Elsewhere in the West and the nation, there wasn’t a huge Week Zero schedule, though there were a couple important games. … No. 14 USC dominated visiting San Jose State for three quarters, then took its foot off the gas and coasted to a 42-26 victory. The Trojans’ freshmen played well. … Stanford roller-coasted its way to a 37-27 win over visiting Hawaii in Tavita Pritchard’s first game as head coach. … Those games attracted a few recruiting visitors. … Oregon has a path to the national title game. … Deion Sanders could certainly use an upset win over Georgia Tech in Colorado’s opening game. … Devon Dampier’s journey at Utah has been anything but smooth. … UCLA has a few former Cal players who are looking forward to their return to Berkeley next weekend. … Arizona State named its starting quarterback. … Arizona will open against a Northern Arizona team that is solid and has a win under its belt. … Finally, a Division II running back, MicahJo Barnett, scored for William Jewell College early in its game with Fort Lewis on Saturday. Not long after he suffered a medical emergency, was rushed to hospital and died.

EWU: Dan Thompson made the long trek to Flagstaff for the Eagles opener and has more than just a game story. He also has a notebook that covers the highs and lows contained in the season-opening loss. … Elsewhere in the Big Sky, sixth-ranked UC Davis fell behind early at Portland State then rallied for a 31-24 victory. … Southern Utah almost made its return to the Big Sky a memorable one before second-ranked Montana rallied to earn the 28-21 win in Kennedy’s head-coaching debut. … No. 1 Montana State traveled to Utah Tech and was awful rude to the hosts, leading 54-0 after three quarters. And at the final gun. … Idaho State shut down VMI in a nonconference matchup, earning a relatively easy 38-10 win. … Weber State won Friday but wants to play better.

Indians: The postseason hopes, slim as they may be, stayed alive Saturday. Spokane earned a 6-3 win in Vancouver. Dave Nichols has the coverage.

Chiefs: One of Spokane’s best players, Gavin Burcar, spent the offseason doing something that will probably make him even better. He played in international competitions. Dave has more in this story.

Velocity: Spokane only had one road win in League One play going into Saturday’s match in Mount Vernon, New York. The Velocity ended the day with two. Three unanswered goals lifted them to a 3-1 victory over WestchesterOK SC.

Mariners: We mentioned the M’s hilarious performance yesterday in a 4-3 come-from-ahead loss to the Blue Jays. We link the game story here again. … Emerson Hancock might have to miss a start…. This year’s top pick is off to a hot start.

Seahawks: Yes, today is cut day. The Hawks’ roster? We linked some thoughts above including Bob Condotta’s in the S-R. We link his again here. … They won’t have to cut Terrion Arnold, who finally signed Saturday. Nor will they be able to practice or play the cornerback as he immediately was put on the commissioner’s exempt list. In other words, he was suspended as his felony charges wind through the Florida legal system. … How did the final preseason game go? So-so.

Sounders: New striker Dejan Joveljić scored twice – on his only two shots – but Seattle only managed a 2-2 draw against Chicago on the road.

Storm: Seattle will play the Sparks today in Los Angeles.

Tennis: The U.S. Open officially begins today. Carlos Alcaraz is the men’s favorite on the court. But Saturday night, the sport’s greatest player of all time, Roger Federer, and one of his greatest storytellers, Mary Carillo, were inducted in the sports Hall of Fame just up the road in Newport, R.I.

Little League: The championship game is this afternoon in Williamsport.
