text:
All NFL 53-man rosters must be determined by 6:00 pm EST on Sunday. All general managers and head coaches will face difficult decisions.

General manager John Lynch and head coach Kyle Shanahan are in the toughest position of all.

That is due to two factors. While all teams play their first games at roughly the same time, the 49ers play theirs the second earliest, on September 10, three days before the main slate. Why is that any more difficult than the Patriots and Seahawks, who play on September 9?

Because the 49ers play in Australia and will be leaving for Down Under on September 2. That is only two days after final cutdowns, and no practices are allowed for three days after the final preseason game.. John Lynch will only have a few days to decide whether to sign any players released by other teams. And, to that end, he and Shanahan will have to project which currently-injured players should be kept and who should receive an injury designation.

There are only two designations the team can use to "save" a player from the 53-man roster. One is the PUP list, but to be eligible, a player must have missed the entirety of training camp. That is why Mykell Williams will be placed on it.

The IR-designated to return list can be used on any player injured during training camp, but the team is allowed only two.

In both instances, the player must sit out a minimum of the first four games of the season.

Here is the conundrum at certain positions.

Offensive line

Heading into training camp, Shanahan and Lynch said the left guard position was an open competition.

The main contenders were Robert Jones, Connor Colby, and Carver Willis. Jones is currently out with an injury, and a time frame has not been given. The Niners tried Austen Pleasants at left guard, though he has mostly played tackle. Early on in that experiment, Pleasants got hurt. While it is supposedly not a serious injury, the timeline adds pressure to the decision.

At center, the initial depth chart had Brett Toth backing up starter Jake Brendel, with Drake Nugent the third stringer. Toth is currently out with a concussion.

On the outside of the offensive line, Vederian Lowe was the likely swing tackle, but he has missed camp with a high ankle sprain. Pleasants and Enrique Cruz are the other backups, but the more experienced Pleasants is hurt.

Are any of those injured linemen—two guards, two tackles, and a center—close enough to returning that they should be kept outright? Are they so far away they should be on the IR list? All have played in at least one practice. (I am not sure if Lowe's partial first practice makes him ineligible for the PUP list.)

How big is the risk of losing a player to another team if he is waived? There are some here who would be attractive backups to other organizations.

Linebacker

The third linebacker position became unsettled when Dee Winters was traded to the Cowboys in the offseason.

Entering training camp, the main contenders were Luke Gifford, who played the position last year and was a Pro Bowler for special teams; Nick Martin, drafted in 2025 but injured much of last year; Garret Wallow, who played well in relief last year; and rookie 5th-round pick Jaden Dugger, who is the most talented of the four.

Gifford has been out for weeks. Martin went down with an injury two games ago. Wallow was out with an injury Thursday night. Dugger was one of the frontrunners to begin with, and he was going to make the team, but probably only one of the others will have a spot. Wallow and Martin have shown promise. Gifford is great on special teams. Will this come down to who will return soonest? If there is a tie in that regard, which one is most likely to clear waivers? (There is no doubt that Shanahan and Lynch want both Martin and Wallow on at least the practice squad.)

So we have four candidates and three injuries.

If a larger pool of IR players were allowed, the situation would be easier, though still difficult.

But the 49ers have to decide only a few days before leaving for Australia who is even able to practice (some of these players are currently in the concussion protocol), let alone play in a game.

And while other GMs and head coaches have the luxury of scanning the waiver wire and having any pickups practice for over a week before the season begins, the Niners will already be acclimating to the time change over 7,000 miles away. Which player can they sign and bring that distance and get up to speed before game day?

I do not envy the kind of situation Lynch and Shanahan are in. No other coach or GM in the league does, either.

title: CHIEFS DRAFT CAPITAL, OR: HOW TO TURN PREMIUM PICKS INTO PREMIUM MEDICAL BILLS
description:
): Felix Anudike-Uzomah (2023 Round 1): Placed on season-ending IR on August 18, 2025, after suffering a catastrophic, severe hamstring tear during preseason camp.
Rashee Rice (2023 Round 2): Placed on season-ending IR following a torn LCL and hamstring tendon damage in Week 4 of the 2024 season.
Wanya Morris (2023 Round 3): Suffered a season-ending knee injury against the Houston Texans in Week 14 of the 2025 season.
Josh Simmons (2025 Round 1): Landed on IR after sustaining a dislocated and fractured wrist in Week 13 against Dallas, requiring major reconstructive surgery.
Because across the NFL, the baseline rate of early-round draft picks (Rounds 1–3) suffering a true season-ending injury during their rookie contract window hovers between 15% and 20%.
text:
I’m not a doctor, but I play one on TV. Maybe you’ve even seen my show - I’m the impossibly handsome resident who’s had a ‘fling’ with every nurse on the ward (except for the token “heavy-set” one with the heart of gold, because I’m way too superficial to be attracted to someone’s personality - SPOILER ALERT!- that won’t happen until season 6). But enough about me (for now, anyway)...

What I’m trying to tell you is that I lack the credentials and training to offer anything meaningful to a discussion about medicine and health (or lack thereof). But, as you by now have probably surmised - I’m going to talk about it anyway.

I’ve been following the news about Josh Simmons’ back problems, and the conspiracy theories that are gaining steam about how he might be exaggerating the injury to avoid playing. I’ve also read the hypothesis (which, rightfully or wrongfully, got over with the Arrowhead Pride fundamentalists about as well as a pregnant pole-vaulter) that Simmons' back problems might be attributable to his off-season weight loss and muscle building program. I’m not going to offer an opinion about that because, as I noted earlier, I’m only a TV doctor. I’ll say this, though - it was actually kind of refreshing to see a Chiefs offensive tackle report to camp not looking like he trained in the off-season at Golden Corral.

Anyway, the discussion about Simmons’ back injury (which followed his season-ending wrist injury, which followed his season-ending torn patellar tendon injury, which followed his season-ending hyperextended earlobe injury) caused me to realize something:

Between the 2023 and 2025 NFL Drafts, the Chiefs made nine selections across the first three rounds - and of those nine premium picks, six have landed on season-ending injured reserve.

I couldn’t even make that up. Here’s what it looks like on paper - presuming you printed this off and filed it in a binder, like many of my readers do. Otherwise you might just be reading it on your phone (Oh, I see how it is - you’re a casual reader. Well… excusez-moi.):

Felix Anudike-Uzomah (2023 Round 1): Placed on season-ending IR on August 18, 2025, after suffering a catastrophic, severe hamstring tear during preseason camp.

Rashee Rice (2023 Round 2): Placed on season-ending IR following a torn LCL and hamstring tendon damage in Week 4 of the 2024 season.

Wanya Morris (2023 Round 3): Suffered a season-ending knee injury against the Houston Texans in Week 14 of the 2025 season.

Kingsley Suamataia (2024 Round 2): Had his campaign cut short by a season-ending ankle injury.

Josh Simmons (2025 Round 1): Landed on IR after sustaining a dislocated and fractured wrist in Week 13 against Dallas, requiring major reconstructive surgery.

Omarr Norman-Lott (2025 Round 2): Tore his right ACL in Week 7 against the Las Vegas Raiders and was placed on season-ending IR on October 21, 2025.

Toss in Ashton Gillotte (2025 Round 3), who’s currently on the shelf with a ruptured plantar fascia (granted, not a season ending injury) in camp, and Xavier Worthy (2024 Round 1), who played the entire 2025 season with one shoulder, and you have yourself a fascinating anomaly.

I know what you must be thinking: What’s an anomaly, Mojo? You know I don’t like it when you use those fancy words!

Sorry…. I forgot about that. An anomaly, simply put, is something that isn’t supposed to happen. Sixty-six percent of the Chiefs’ nine selections across the first three rounds in 2023, 2024, and 2025 have landed on season-ending injured reserve. That - isn’t supposed to happen.

Why do I say that?

Because across the NFL, the baseline rate of early-round draft picks (Rounds 1–3) suffering a true season-ending injury during their rookie contract window hovers between 15% and 20%.

Now, the nitpicker in you (not to be confused with the ‘nosepicker’ in you) will inevitably point to the calendar and claim that some of these designations were administrative conveniences—that guys like Wanya Morris or Josh Simmons only landed on IR because their injuries happened in December when only a handful of regular-season games remained. Go ahead - say it. You know you want to.... Because that’s just what you do, isn't it! You refuse to accept anything I say at face value!! It’s okay. I don’t take personally…. NOSEPICKER!!!

Anyway, that argument completely ignores the surgical reality of the injuries.

When Simmons fractured and dislocated his wrist against Dallas in Week 13, he underwent a complex surgical repair requiring multi-month recovery and rehab. When Morris got rolled up on against the Texans, his knee suffered severe structural trauma requiring full repair. These weren’t your typical, garden-variety soft-tissue tweaks - even if these injuries had occurred in Week 2 or Week 6, they would have ended a season.

And no, I didn’t perform the surgeries. I’m just a TV doctor.

So you might ask: What’s the root cause of all this, Mojo? And I’ll say the same thing to you that I always said to my 9th grade chemistry teacher when she called on me to answer a question in class - “I dunno.... -under my breath- you hateful shrew.”

And I don’t know.

Not for certain.

And I also realize that must come as a complete shock to you because you’ve always operated on the assumption that I know everything about everything.

“Mojo, I feel so disillusioned. I can’t believe in anything anymore!!!!”

What I can infer is that picking at the tail end of the round for the better part of the last decade has led Brett Veach and Andy Reid to take some calculated gambles on players with a premier ceiling over clean medical histories. And that’s understandable - to an extent. We've all bought Ferraris with salvage titles at some point in our lives. And sometimes that strategy can work out magnificently cough cough Trey Smith cough cough. But when six out of nine top selections across three consecutive drafts either lose a full year to major surgery or play through a torn joint capsule, you aren't just dealing with normal football attrition.

You're watching an episode of M*A*S*H.

And even M*A*S*H. eventually got cancelled, so maybe it’s time to switch things up a little.

title: 2026 NFL Preseason, Week 3: What We Learned from Friday's games
authors: Nick Shook, Jeremy Bergman, Bobby Kownack
description:
Both had nondescript games, though Pocic's holding penalty on a long catch-and-run pushed Baltimore out of field-goal range on one drive.
It's looking like Gwyn's job in place of the injured Danny Pinter for Week 1, unless there's a Labor Day development.
Tua Tagovailoa's preseason finale represented a bit of progress even if the stats don't tell the whole story.
Getting another preseason start, rookie QB Cade Klubnik (6-of-13, 59 yards) didn't do much to enhance his QB2 candidacy.
There’s fullback Adam Prentice, who plunged past the goal line for a 1-yard score versus Minnesota, his second of the preseason.
text:
Ravens' depth chart taking shape? Chris Moore made a strong case Friday to be included on the initial 53-man roster. The journeyman 33-year-old hauled in three passes from Tyler Huntley for 54 yards, including a highlight-reel diving TD grab, on the Ravens' first drive. Moore looked at ease on the outside, playing just two drives alongside fellow down-chart WRs Devontez Walker and LaJohntay Wester, who is an asset in the return game and made an impressive adjustment on a TD catch Friday night. Missing from the opening lineup was fourth-rounder Elijah Sarratt. The ex-Hoosier was a non-factor on offense against Washington and served as the Ravens' second returner. What's his role on this roster? Baltimore's WR depth is set at the top. Zay Flowers just got paid, and Ja'Kobi Lane was the breakout star of camp. Both wideouts sat out Friday, as did Rashod Bateman, whose in-season availability may be in jeopardy due to a June arrest. ... Baltimore's center battle continued into the final week of the preseason. Jovaughn Gwyn started again, playing two drives before ceding the half to Ethan Pocic. Both had nondescript games, though Pocic's holding penalty on a long catch-and-run pushed Baltimore out of field-goal range on one drive. It's looking like Gwyn's job in place of the injured Danny Pinter for Week 1, unless there's a Labor Day development. ... A lingering issue: Tyler Loop missed two field goals from over 50 yards against Washington, his third miss from at least 49 this summer. Not a good omen for the kicker whose 44-yard miss in Week 18 ended Baltimore's 2025 season.

-- Jeremy Bergman

Tagovailoa enjoys minor improvement. Tua Tagovailoa's preseason finale represented a bit of progress even if the stats don't tell the whole story. The first drive saw Tagovailoa complete a couple of passes, but the big gainer came via a tight end screen to Kyle Pitts, a short throw that Pitts took 37 yards to set up Atlanta's first scoring opportunity. He finished 7-of-8 passing for 95 yards but also turned it over once when he fumbled a snap. It's better than earlier outings, but Kevin Stefanski and OC Tommy Rees also kept things simple and minimized risk. Overall, Tagovailoa didn't do much to convince anyone he should be the Falcons' starter unless Michael Penix Jr. can't play.

Bell is the focus in Miami. The talk of Dolphins camp has revolved around the blossoming of third-year edge rusher Chop Robinson and the surprisingly quick emergence of rookie Chris Bell. Though it's only preseason football, Miami's offensive priority was clear Friday night: Get the ball to Bell. Through three possessions, Bell led the Dolphins in targets with five. He was often the first target backup Cam Miller looked for immediately after the snap, and while he only finished with two catches, it was easy to recognize why Miami values the rookie and how he'll be a priority in their passing game all season long. All that's left is to advance to the regular season and let Bell get to work with quarterback Malik Willis.

-- Nick Shook

Jags UDFA defensive end continues push for roster spot. Bryan Thomas Jr., Jacksonville’s undrafted rookie out of South Carolina, is so under the radar that Google can only think to redirect searches toward Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. The defensive end has steadily been making a name for himself this preseason, though. Thomas entered Friday night with seven tackles, five pressures and a sack across his previous two contests. He added another four tackles, four pressures and 2.5 sacks against the Buccaneers. On his first sack, Thomas burst past offensive lineman Elijah Klein around the edge to take down Jalon Daniels and end Tampa Bay’s drive toward the end of the first half. He swam past Klein on the inside on another QB takedown a quarter later, and his half sack in the final frame was all hustle. The Jags rested a large portion of starters for much of the preseason, affording opportunities to players like Thomas. He’s made the most of it, but will there be room in Jacksonville for two BTJs?

Daniels doesn’t grab QB2 opportunity. Tampa Bay had an unexpected backup quarterback competition on its hands this August after Jalon Daniels played himself into the conversation. The undrafted free agent impressed in his two previous appearances, going a combined 19 of 29 for 182 yards and a touchdown, plus another rushing score with 28 yards on 10 carries. He was given the start in the Buccaneers’ preseason finale, a legitimate chance to prove he deserves to be the guy behind Baker Mayfield. For the first time, Daniels didn’t look nearly up to the task. He saw multiple drives end on third-down drops, but Daniels wasn’t doing himself any favors, either. Over the course of seven drives, he threw for 57 yards on 8-of-15 passing. His only possession that didn’t end in a punt was cut short because he fumbled a snap under center. Jake Browning similarly delivered a clunker -- he went 2 of 4 for 2 yards over three possessions, a couple of which were sabotaged by penalties -- but he could still potentially get the nod as the veteran in the room.

-- Bobby Kownack

Veterans battle for roster spots on Giants offense. Odell Beckham, on the fringe of the roster, was under the spotlight Friday night. OBJ was bodied on an early Jameis Winston interception but responded with three strong catches (53 yards) that moved the chains. Once a human highlight reel, Beckham nearly contributed again when he got free on a second-quarter deep shot, but his version of the helmet catch was not to be, in part thanks to a Winston overthrow. Elsewhere on the depth chart, a fumble by Braxton Berrios deep in the red zone may have harmed his candidacy, though he projects as New York's returner with Calvin Austin injured. OBJ put his best foot forward Friday and throughout the summer. Will John Harbaugh and Joe Schoen reward the vet with a roster spot? ... At running back, summer acquisition Najee Harris and Tyrone Tracy Jr. went snap for snap at the start of the game. Harris ran hard (39 yards on 11 carries), while Tracy found burst (9.3 YPC) and the end zone. Unfortunately, Tracy went to the locker room to be evaluated for a head injury in the second quarter. He was cleared but did not return, bringing an early end to his rough preseason. Behind Cam Skattebo, there should be an odd man out in New York's RB room between Harris, Tracy and Devin Singletary. Who will it be come cutdown day?

Minor turbulence for Jets. After a shutout of Pittsburgh the week prior, the Jets flew through some dirty air on Friday night. Getting another preseason start, rookie QB Cade Klubnik (6-of-13, 59 yards) didn't do much to enhance his QB2 candidacy. His underthrow of big target Jelani Woods on an interception was an unfortunate error. Klubnik's mobility made up for breakdowns in play, but against Giants backups, he didn't necessarily look ready for prime time. ... Joseph Ossai saw his first preseason action since signing a $36 million deal in the offseason but had to leave with a foot injury. A notable free-agent acquisition, Ossai is critical to improving New York's pass rush but has not been available much this offseason. ... Jason Sanders, who won the place-kicking job this week over Cade York, missed an extra points and a 54-yard field goal. Whoops.

-- Jeremy Bergman

Saints offense humming as regular season approaches. Kellen Moore's crew found an impressive rhythm in Arlington on Friday night, expressing schematic creativity by relying on an assortment of athletes who figure to play a notable (if not larger) role in 2026. Rookie Barion Brown took a jet sweep around the right end for a touchdown, backup quarterback Spencer Rattler kept a read option and won the race to the pylon for a score, Kendre Miller ran hard in perhaps his final chance to win a roster spot, and Audric Estimé ripped off a 33-yarder to set up Rattler's touchdown just before half. Plenty of offenses keep things generally monotonous in the preseason, but Moore's unit adopted an aggressive approach that earned advantages on the edge, produced points and exposed a few potentially important contributors prior to the start of the regular season. When it comes to tune-ups, New Orleans' offense handled this one properly.

-- Nick Shook

Lemon drop mars debut. First-round pick Makai Lemon saw his first preseason action after missing most of training camp with a hamstring injury. He was targeted right away by Tanner McKee, getting free on an out route for an easy 3-yard gain. A deep shot to Lemon two plays later was deflected by the defender. Then, on his fourth target, Lemon couldn't corral a dart from McKee on a slant, the ball deflecting off his hands for an interception. After Lemon saw 17 offensive snaps (three catches on five targets for 3 yards), Philly oddly tossed him back out there for a third-quarter punt return. The former Trojan played half of snaps out wide and half in the slot, perhaps providing a glimpse at the versatility he'll provide Jalen Hurts alongside DeVonta Smith in the starting offense. For a player who thrived in college at playing in the middle of the field, Lemon's big drop and little gains were letdowns, but any action is better than no action.

Meyers shines again. One of the stories of Bengals camp has been Dohnte Meyers, a 26-year-old former CFLer who's been turning heads. On Friday night, he did it in prime time. Meyers caught three passes against Philly, all of which came with great separation and went for first downs. He leaves the preseason with a team-best 11 receptions for 121 yards. Behind Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, Joe Burrow may have himself another inside man.

-- Jeremy Bergman

Dennis-Sutton dangerous in first preseason action. Packers fourth-round pass rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton made an early splash in his lone preseason appearance. Seven plays into his debut, Dennis-Sutton split Cardinals offensive linemen Jayden Williams and Matt Pryor on a stunt, was much too explosive for Pryor to pick up and quickly closed the gap to throw Gardner Minshew to the ground and set up a third-and-20, slowing an Arizona drive that had been moving at that point. Dennis-Sutton was too early anticipating the snap on the very next play, incurring an offside penalty, but that’s life as a rookie. He got close a few more times throughout the night, disrupting multiple plays with four pressures. While he’s a little late to the game in terms of cracking the starting edge rotation after missing time due to a heat-related illness, it was a good initial showing, and Green Bay will need all hands on deck as it looks to sustain a pass rush amid Micah Parsons’ absence to begin the season. … Will Sheppard and J. Michael Sturdivant, undrafted free agents from 2025 and ’26, respectively, made compelling cases for the 53-man roster. Sheppard collected three receptions for 26 yards and a score, but more impressively sent Lambeau Field into a frenzy with an 81-yard punt-return touchdown. Sturdivant tallied 112 yards and a TD on six catches. It would potentially take Green Bay keeping seven wide receivers for either to make the roster, but the two hopefuls certainly gave the team something to think about.

Minshew deserves firm grip on backup gig. Carson Beck was all the rage after his performance in the Hall of Fame Game, but the third-round rookie hasn’t played since. Gardner Minshew has, and he’s displayed the goods that make him one of the more valuable backup quarterbacks in the league. His latest such display took place on Friday against the Packers. Minshew played two drives, a 66-yard march for a field goal and an 85-yard sprint that he capped off with a 41-yard touchdown strike to Simi Fehoko. He was done for the night after that with 126 yards and a sterling 155.8 passer rating on 7-of-9 passing. If the Cardinals need to turn to a QB behind Jacoby Brissett this season, who they select will likely depend heavily on context. Minshew, the gutsy vet with 47 career starts, would give them the most consistency should an injury arise early, but there’s a possibility Arizona will be in a situation where it wants to see what it has in Beck at some point late in the season.

-- Bobby Kownack

Broncos have some tough decisions. Denver’s three running back spots are a lock: J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey and Jonah Coleman. If the Broncos keep a fourth ball-carrier, who will it be? There’s fullback Adam Prentice, who plunged past the goal line for a 1-yard score versus Minnesota, his second of the preseason. Tyler Badie and Jaleel McLaughlin have both played roles in Sean Payton’s offenses before, and they did some good things on Friday. Badie had an impressively shifty run for 10 yards, finishing with 24 on six carries, while McLaughlin was characteristically useful in the passing game. McLaughlin blazed through the middle of Minnesota’s defense on a 20-yard TD reception and finished with 35 yards on six catches. Even Cody Schrader had a big night, racking up 132 yards and a score on 19 touches. There’s also the quarterback question. Jarrett Stidham was treated as the victor of the backup job, leading two scoring drives before giving way to Sam Ehlinger. Will the Broncos keep three there or try to sneak Ehlinger on the practice squad? The 27-year-old played the remainder of the game and put a ton on tape that will interest other suitors. He led a nice 65-yard two-minute TD drill before half, later had a highlight-reel touchdown pass that required buying time for over 6.5 seconds and scrambling 28.1 yards, per Next Gen Stats, and bought time again on the next drive before tossing an 88-yard TD on a terribly blown coverage by the Vikings. He finished an impressive 15 of 20 for 233 yards, three scores and an interception.

-- Bobby Kownack

title: Chiefs Dealt Unfortunate News 16 Days Before Start of NFL Season vs. Broncos
description:
Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons is dealing with a back injury.
Reid noted that Simmons’ injury could “take a little bit of time” to heal.
It is less than ideal news with the NFL season nearly two weeks away from starting.
Now, Simmons’ status for Week 1 could be in doubt if the left tackle is not able to recover soon.
“They have Jaylon Moore who’s kind of like their swing, right tackle, left tackle.
text:
The Kansas City Chiefs‘ preseason if officially over and now the attention turns to Week 1. First, the Chiefs will need to finalize the team’s roster ahead of the NFL deadline on Sunday, August 30.

Additionally, the Chiefs continue to deal with injury concerns for one of the team’s key players. Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons is dealing with a back injury.

Head coach Andy Reid was vague about Simmons’ potential return timeline but indicated that the tackle remains in pain. Reid noted that Simmons’ injury could “take a little bit of time” to heal.

It is less than ideal news with the NFL season nearly two weeks away from starting.

“It’s going to take a little bit of time here, but he’s a hard worker when it comes to these type of things,” Reid told reporters on August 28.

“… It’s just a matter of eliminating some of the pain that he has and (assessing his) strength. Making sure he has enough strength there.”

Chiefs News: Kansas City Is Assessing Whether LT Josh Simmons Is Dealing With a Long-Term Injury

The news comes as Patrick Mahomes is set to return from a season-ending ACL injury. Protecting Mahomes is of high importance, and Simmons is expected to be responsible for the quarterback’s blindside.

Now, Simmons’ status for Week 1 could be in doubt if the left tackle is not able to recover soon. ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler reported that the Chiefs are assessing whether Simmons is dealing with a long-term injury.

“Josh Simmons, this one is interesting because he’s got a back issue,” Fowler explained on an August 27, edition of “SportsCenter.” “He’s been classified as day to day, but I can say that he is undergoing more tests to see if there is something long term here. So this could be one to watch.

“They have Jaylon Moore who’s kind of like their swing, right tackle, left tackle. He could start there if needed. So, (the injury) could be minor, but they’re still identifying that situation,” Fowler continued.

“That would be big. They’re a much better offense when he’s in there.”

The Chiefs Face Offensive Line Questions Amid Patrick Mahomes’ Return

Kansas City has high hopes for Simmons after selecting the offensive lineman in the first round of the 2025 NFL draft. Yet, Simmons played just eight games during his rookie season in 2025.

It would be less than ideal for Simmons to miss time to start the season. This is especially true with Mahomes returning from a serious injury.

Mahomes previously stated that Simmons has a chance to be one of the NFL’s top left tackles.

“He’s a ‘dawg’ at the end of the day,” Mahomes noted on an August 2025, interview on “Up and Adams,” via On3. “I mean, he’s obviously working through being an NFL pro and being a veteran, but when it comes to just pass blocking and run blocking, he can get the job done.

“… I think it’s just you hear the defensive guys talk about him, and they all are saying the right things when you want a guy that’s going to go out there and contribute,” Mahomes added.

“And so, the sky’s the limit. He has a chance to be one of the best there is at that left tackle position, but he’s got to go out there and prove that in the regular season.”

title: Commanders final 53-man roster projection: Tough choice at WR, help needed on O-line
description:
The Commanders’ revamped roster showed promise early in training camp, especially on defense, where the team made its biggest offseason investments.
That also made the team’s initial 53-man roster, due by 6 p.m. Sunday, vulnerable to significant change before that first game.
My initial roster projection for Washington is just that — an early iteration but not the final roster for Week 1.
(Note: NFL teams can designate for return up to two players who are placed on injured reserve on roster cutdown day.
Those count toward teams’ maximum of eight IR players designated for return, but do not count against the team’s roster cap.
text:
In the 237 days since last season ended, the Commanders have overhauled their systems, replaced their play callers, and changed some of their coaching staff and much of their roster in hopes of rediscovering a winning formula.

The team that made it to the NFC Championship Game two years ago is once again in rebuild mode — but with higher stakes. Coach Dan Quinn’s future in Washington may depend on a winning season, and the window to build around quarterback Jayden Daniels while he’s on his rookie contract will soon close.

The Commanders’ revamped roster showed promise early in training camp, especially on defense, where the team made its biggest offseason investments. But a slew of injuries to starters and some key reserves limited their on-field work together and created uncertainty about who will be available when the season opens Sept. 13 in Philadelphia.

That also made the team’s initial 53-man roster, due by 6 p.m. Sunday, vulnerable to significant change before that first game. Washington is seventh in the NFL’s waiver list priority order, which means it’ll have a fairly early crack at claiming, say, an interior offensive lineman (or two) or landing other quality players waived by other teams.

My initial roster projection for Washington is just that — an early iteration but not the final roster for Week 1.

(Note: NFL teams can designate for return up to two players who are placed on injured reserve on roster cutdown day. Those count toward teams’ maximum of eight IR players designated for return, but do not count against the team’s roster cap. They are eligible to return after four games. Anyone else placed on injured reserve before the 6 p.m. deadline on Sunday is done for the season.)

Offense (26)

Quarterback (3): Jayden Daniels, Marcus Mariota, Athan Kaliakmanis

Hey, shocker, Daniels is still the starter! In all seriousness, Daniels had an exceptional camp. He’s shown more and more every offseason, but this one was especially notable because of the new scheme and all that he was asked to change or do more of in offensive coordinator David Blough’s system. His transition to playing more under center appeared seamless, and his command of the offense was what you’d expect from a veteran with multiple years in a scheme.

Mariota returned on a one-year deal, ensuring continuity in the quarterback room amid all the other offensive changes.

The notable name here, though, is Kaliakmanis, a seventh-round rookie from Rutgers whose play in the first two preseason games earned him a spot here. Washington kept three quarterbacks on its initial roster the last two seasons, and with Mariota recovering from an MCL sprain, doing so again may be wise. Quinn has said he’s optimistic the veteran will be available for Week 1, but it’s not yet a certainty.

Whether Kaliakmanis sticks at the No. 3 for the season may depend on who comes available after roster cuts.

Running back (3): Jacory “Bill” Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White, Kaytron Allen

Washington released veteran Jerome Ford with an injury settlement and Jeremy McNichols suffered a “pretty good quad injury” in camp, according to Quinn. I didn’t include him on the belief he would clear waivers and be available to re-sign to the practice squad.

Allen had an up-and-down preseason — he had 85 rushing yards and a touchdown against Miami but fumbled on Washington’s opening snap in Baltimore — but his potential and draft status (sixth-round pick) ensure he stays. Undrafted rookie Robert Henry impressed in the opener against Miami, but he may not have shown enough to put Washington at risk of losing him on waivers.

Wide receiver (7): Terry McLaurin, Stefon Diggs, Antonio Williams, Treylon Burks, Dyami Brown, Jaylin Lane, Luke McCaffrey

Receiver was one of Washington’s most questionable positions before training camp, but the arrival of Diggs turned it into one of the most competitive.

McLaurin, Diggs and third-round rookie Williams were locks for the roster, leaving eight wideouts vying for three or four spots. Brown got the nod because of his speed and rapport with Daniels. Burks’ big-play ability won him a spot, and Lane made it because of his punt returns. I admittedly waffled about keeping McCaffrey. He had a very good camp and doubles as the team’s leading kick returner, but I wondered if he showed enough to hold his spot. I kept him because of his draft status (third round in 2024), his consistency compared to others and the value he provides over, say, a fifth linebacker or 10th offensive lineman.

Tight end (4): Chig Okonkwo, John Bates, Ben Sinnott, Colson Yankoff

It was always going to be these four. Yankoff had a good camp, showing his pass-catching ability on offense while remaining a special teams staple, and the others were locks before camp opened.

Offensive line (9): LT Brandon Coleman, LG Chris Paul, C Nick Allegretti, RG Sam Cosmi, RT Josh Conerly Jr., OT Andrew Wylie, OL Trent Scott, D.J. Humphries, C Matt Gulbin

*Laremy Tunsil placed on injured reserve with a designation to return

This is the group that figures to change before the opener. It needs to change. Washington cut center Tyler Biadasz in February and didn’t sign another veteran in the offseason, essentially leaving the job to Allegretti, a versatile vet who has played primarily guard. But a calf injury sidelined Allegretti for almost all of camp and his status for the opener is still not clear. Also unclear: His ability as a full-time starter at center.

Julian Good-Jones and Gulbin, a sixth-round rookie, struggled mightily in place of Allegretti, hindering the run game and leaving Daniels exposed for much of the Commanders’ joint practice with the Ravens.

Gulbin stays on the roster largely because the team invested a draft pick in him, but it wasn’t a high enough one to keep him here long-term. Washington should add another center and more help at guard since Coleman shifted back outside to left tackle after Tunsil’s injury.

Tunsil is an obvious candidate for IR with a designation for return on cutdown day. He underwent surgery to repair a torn triceps on Aug. 8, but the team left open the possibility of him returning this season. That injury typically has a 3 to 4-month recovery, depending on the severity and type of repair.

Defense (24)

Defensive line (6): Daron Payne, Javon Kinlaw, Tim Settle, Charles Omenihu, Shy Tuttle, Byron Cowart

*Johnny Newton is placed on IR with a designation to return.

Newton’s pectoral muscle injury will land him on IR, but, like Tunsil, there’s still a chance he could be available later this season, so designating him for return on cutdown day keeps the door open for Washington.

The Commanders brought back Settle and signed Omenihu to add needed depth at the position. Newton’s injury pushes Tuttle up as the top reserve.

Cowart gets the last spot because of his experience, but like others near the bottom of the depth chart, his spot could change depending on roster needs and who becomes available.

Linebacker (4): Frankie Luvu, Sonny Styles, Leo Chenal, Jordan Magee

There are no real surprises here. Kain Medrano and Ale Kaho were possibilities for a fifth linebacker spot, but both seem likely to clear waivers, meaning Washington could sign them back to the practice squad and continue to develop them and have them ready for a few game-day call-ups.

Outside linebacker (4): Odafe Oweh, K’Lavon Chaisson, Joshua Josephs, Javontae Jean-Baptiste

*Dorance Armstrong is placed on the reserve/suspended list

The NFL suspended Armstrong for the season opener for violating the personal conduct policy, which temporarily clears a roster spot. Jean-Baptiste missed much of last season due to a pectoral injury and didn’t show much in the early going of camp. If Washington’s outside linebackers finished camp healthy and available, Jean-Baptiste may have been hard-pressed to get a spot, but Armstrong’s suspension and injuries to Oweh (calf) and Chaisson (knee) — Quinn has not provided a timetable for their return — make it worth keeping him.

Cornerback (5): Mike Sainristil, Amik Robertson, Trey Amos, Rasul Douglas, Fabian Moreau

There are a number of outstanding questions about this group, none bigger than the availability of Amos. The 2025 second-round pick was Washington’s most consistent corner last year, but a fractured fibula cut his season short and cost him the entire offseason. He returned two weeks into camp but suffered an ankle sprain in his second practice. It’s unclear if he will be available for Week 1.

Washington added Douglas and Moreau to give the team more veteran experience and depth, and both proved their worth.

Whenever Amos returns, it’ll be interesting to see whether Robertson or Sainristil shifts inside to the slot.

Safety (5): Nick Cross, Jeremy Reaves, Quan Martin, Percy Butler, Tyler Owens

Washington’s most notable roster cut happened Tuesday. Will Harris was the team’s top safety during his limited time last season (he missed eight games because of a fractured fibula), but the addition of Cross in free agency pushed him down the depth chart. Butler and Owens have been staples on special teams and became even more important when special teams ace Nick Bellore retired.

Martin struggled last season, but his two preseason interceptions made the decision to move on from Harris an obvious one.

Special teams (3)

P/H Tress Way, K Drew Stevens, LS Tyler Ott
